title: Agincourt Without the Myths
standfirst: What the sources say about the battle, and what they leave out.

readingList.title: Why the Romans Feared Their Own Generals

body: Few battles are as wrapped in legend as Agincourt. On 25 October 1415, a tired English army under Henry V defeated a much larger French force in northern France. Shakespeare turned it into a story of a band of brothers. The sources tell a messier and more interesting tale.

Every account agrees that the English were outnumbered. By how much is still argued over. Some chroniclers give the French army a size several times larger than the English one. Modern historians who have worked through the muster rolls have suggested the gap may have been smaller than the legend claims. The English were at a real disadvantage, but perhaps not the impossible one of popular memory.
## The ground did much of the work

The battle was fought on a narrow strip of freshly ploughed land between two woods, soaked by heavy rain. French men-at-arms advancing in heavy armour sank into the mud and were funnelled into a crush. The English archers, protected by sharpened stakes, poured arrows into the packed ranks.
Once the French front line stalled, those behind pushed forward into it. Many men seem to have died in the press, unable to fight or get away.
## The part the legend leaves out

During the battle, fearing a fresh attack, Henry ordered many French prisoners to be killed. Chroniclers on both sides recorded it. It sits awkwardly beside the heroic version of the day, which is perhaps why it is so often forgotten.
Agincourt was a remarkable victory. It was also a muddy, frightening and brutal fight, decided as much by weather and ground as by valour.
